rules.title: Four waits bound a connection, all finite with nothing configured and all idle rather than total
rules.diverges: `max_execution_time` and `request_terminate_timeout` bound a whole request; these bound a stalled socket only, so a slow 2 GB upload completes while a stalled one is closed

rules.title: An `accept` that fails on descriptor exhaustion is retried under a bounded backoff and logged once per window

sections.title: Resolving a request
sections.blurb: Five steps from bytes to entry point, forwarded headers that are read only from a trusted peer, and a trailing slash that means something.

rules.title: A request resolves by longest mount match, prefix strip, static file, path dispatch, then the entry — and production runs only match, strip, entry
rules.diverges: `try_files $uri /index.php` is the development sequence only; in production a URL naming an existing `.nvs` file still runs the mount's entry

rules.title: `trusted_proxies` defaults to empty, empty means the forwarded headers are never read, and a trusted walk takes the rightmost untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` entry
rules.diverges: `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']` and `HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR` are replaced by one `clientIp(): ?tainted string`, which is the socket peer until an operator names the proxies

rules.title: `X-Forwarded-For` is the only client-address header read; a trusted peer sending another is warned about, and an untrusted header is ignored, never refused
rules.diverges: `X-Real-IP`, `CF-Connecting-IP`, `True-Client-IP`, `Fastly-Client-IP`, `X-Client-IP` and RFC 7239 `Forwarded` are never read, so the common `proxy_set_header X-Real-IP` recipe alone leaves every client as the proxy

rules.title: A forwarded token's port is removed, a withheld address answers `null`, and a token that neither names nor withholds one is a `400`
rules.diverges: `clientIp()` is nullable and `null` is an answer, never repaired to `""` or `0.0.0.0`

rules.title: A trusted `X-Forwarded-Proto` sets the effective scheme and HSTS emission and feeds nothing else; no `X-Forwarded-Host` is read
rules.diverges: `$_SERVER['HTTPS']` is `Core\Request::scheme()`, set only by a trusted proxy, and a redirect never reconstructs a scheme from it

rules.title: An absent `Host` is a `400`; matching strips the port, folds ASCII case and one trailing dot, refuses non-ASCII, and an unknown host on a host-mounted deployment is a `404`
rules.diverges: there is no `ALLOWED_HOSTS`-style allowlist and no `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']`: the host mounts are the allowlist, and nginx must send `proxy_set_header Host $host`

rules.title: A filesystem path is never derived from a URL at request time
rules.diverges: `cgi.fix_pathinfo`, `SCRIPT_FILENAME` and `PATH_INFO` have no counterpart: a request selects a mount from a table expanded at boot and can never name a file

rules.title: A trailing slash is never normalised: `/users` and `/users/` are two URIs
rules.diverges: no `DirectorySlash`, no framework redirect and no `rtrim($uri, '/')`: whether the two name one resource is the application's knowledge

sections.title: Methods, bodies and static files
sections.blurb: HEAD runs as GET, a preflight is answered before any code runs, and a route that never reads a body allocates nothing.

rules.title: `HEAD` runs as `GET` with the body discarded and `Content-Length` kept; `method()` reports `Get` and `isHead()` tells the truth
rules.diverges: `$_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']` would say `HEAD`; `Core\Request::method()` says `Get` so the route matches, and `isHead()` is the only place the difference shows

rules.title: A CORS preflight is answered from `[http.cors]` before the unit is loaded, and a plain `OPTIONS` is passed through
rules.diverges: no `header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin: …')` in application code answers a preflight; the policy answers it before the program exists

rules.title: `[limits] request_body` bounds bytes parsed into memory and `upload_total` bounds a streamed multipart body, each with a hard ceiling, and a route that never reads a body allocates nothing
rules.diverges: `upload_max_filesize`, `post_max_size` and `$_FILES['tmp_name']` have no counterpart: there is no temp file, `Core\Request::files()` yields streams, and a route raises its own cap before reading

rules.title: A buffering body reader keeps what it read so another may follow it, and a streaming one consumes the body and is the only reader of it
rules.diverges: `$_POST` is populated before the program runs and leaves `php://input` empty for a multipart body; here nothing is read until a member asks, and which reader may follow which is stated rather than decided by `enable_post_data_reading`

rules.title: Static serving is one policy in both modes: the exact file, never a listing, one `ETag`, one `Range`, and a `.nvs` file is never served as source
rules.diverges: there is no `Last-Modified`, no directory index, no `.htaccess` and no `max-age`; `php -S` serving any file under the root, source included, has no counterpart

rules.title: `health_path` is off by default; set, it answers `200` while accepting and `503` while draining, and checks no dependency
rules.diverges: php-fpm's `ping.path` and `pm.status_path` have a counterpart that reports no status page, no version and no pool statistics

rules.title: The trace id exists on every request regardless of sampling, is the only request identifier, is emitted on the response, and an inbound `X-Request-ID` is ignored
rules.diverges: there is no `X-Request-ID` and no `$_SERVER['UNIQUE_ID']`; the W3C trace id is the one identifier on every log line, error page and response

sections.title: Response headers, CORS and cookies
sections.blurb: What a deployment that configured nothing already sends, and why CORS stays closed until an origin is named.

rules.title: `[log] access` is a mode default — on in development, off in production — and a `5xx` is logged whatever it says
rules.diverges: there is no Common or Combined Log Format and no pool `access.log`: the line is a diagnostic record, text in development and JSON in production

rules.title: A deployment that wrote no `[http.headers]` already sends `nosniff`, `frame-ancestors 'none'` and a referrer policy on every response
rules.diverges: a php-fpm response carries none of these unless the nginx server block or the application adds them; here they are on every response with nothing configured, and there is no default `Content-Security-Policy` beyond `frame-ancestors`

rules.title: HSTS is emitted when the effective scheme is `https` and not otherwise, and `hsts_subdomains` defaults to `false`
CORS is closed until `[http.cors] origins` names one: no header is emitted and a preflight is answered `403`
rules.diverges: PHP has no CORS default at all, so a preflight nobody handled is whatever the route does; here it is a `403` until an origin is written

rules.title: `origins = ["*"]` with `credentials = true` is refused at boot and at runtime alike, and so is `same_site = "None"` without `secure`
rules.diverges: `header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *')` beside `Allow-Credentials: true` is accepted by PHP and silently rejected by every browser; here the pair does not boot and `Core\Config::set` will not form it

rules.title: Every cookie `Core\Response::addCookie` writes is `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` unless the call site says otherwise
rules.diverges: `setcookie` defaults to no `Secure`, no `HttpOnly` and no `SameSite`; here every cookie starts with all three, `SameSite` is an enum rather than a string, and a script-readable cookie is one written field at the call

rules.title: Every `[http.headers]`, `[http.cors]` and `[http.cookies]` directive is `Runtime` class, and `Core\Response::setHeader` overrides a policy-owned header on one response without logging

sections.title: Sessions
sections.blurb: A session is a record its store issued. Four operations, loaded once, written whole only when it changed, and never locked.

rules.title: A session is a record its store issued: a backend answers `issue`, `load`, `save` and `destroy`, and `load` answering absent is the whole of the strict-id rule
rules.diverges: there is no `SessionHandlerInterface` and no `validateId`; an id the store never issued, one that expired and one an attacker minted are all the same absent answer, and `start` issues a fresh record for each

rules.title: `[session] backend` admits `shared` and `db`, and writing `local` is a boot refusal naming the file it was written in
rules.diverges: `session.save_handler = files` and an APCu-backed handler have no counterpart; the choices are the shared tier or the database, and `local` is `E0626` where it is written rather than a session that forgets people

rules.title: A tree with no `[session]` block has no session store, and `start` throws naming the block to write
rules.diverges: `session_start()` with nothing configured writes files under `session.save_path`; here a store nobody chose is no store, and the first `start` says which block would choose one

rules.title: A session record is loaded once at `start`, written back whole only when it changed, and never locked
rules.diverges: PHP holds an exclusive lock on the session for the length of the request, so two requests from one browser serialize; here there is no lock, and two concurrent writes to one session are last-write-wins over the whole record

rules.title: `[session] ttl` is written onto the record and the store expires it; there is no sweeper and no probability of one
rules.diverges: `session.gc_probability` and `session.gc_divisor` have no counterpart, because both backends can expire an entry themselves and a filesystem cannot

rules.title: A user's own secret lives in their session, sealed under a key ring through `setSecret` and `getSecret`
rules.diverges: `$_SESSION` holds whatever it is given in the clear, and a token in it is readable by anything that can read the store

sections.title: Uploads
sections.blurb: Parts arrive lazily through one member, bounded by two separate caps, and there is no temporary file anywhere.

rules.title: `Core\Request::files()` yields uploaded parts lazily, one at a time, and is the only way to receive one
rules.diverges: there is no `$_FILES` array and no buffered accessor beside the iterator; every application that accepts a file writes a `foreach`, and a part's bytes are readable once, in order

rules.title: A part is a file part iff its `Content-Disposition` carries `filename`; every other part is buffered into `post()`
rules.diverges: a part answers `name()`, `filename()` and `contentType()` as tainted strings through members, and there is no `size`, no `tmp_name` and no `error` slot

rules.title: A part is consumed by `readAll`, by walking `content()`, or by `saveTo`, and each way is bounded
rules.diverges: `move_uploaded_file` is `saveTo`, `file_get_contents($tmp)` is `readAll` under `request_body`, and a second pass over an upload has to say where the first one put it

rules.title: `request_body` caps bytes parsed into memory and `upload_total` caps a streamed multipart body, and both are `[limits]` rows
rules.diverges: `upload_max_filesize` and `post_max_size` are replaced by a cap on what is parsed into memory and a cap on what is streamed past it, and a file's size is never checked against the first

rules.title: `upload_total` is enforced by the server on the wire: a declared oversize is refused before dispatch and a chunked one is stopped at the part being read
There is no temp file: a part lands on disk only where the application names a path under `fs.write`, and disk is the resource it must bound
rules.diverges: there is no `tmp_name`, no `upload_tmp_dir`, no `move_uploaded_file` and no `is_uploaded_file`; an upload nobody saves is never on disk, and one that is saved is there because the program wrote it

sections.title: The HTTP client
sections.blurb: No spelling for "wait forever", one deadline over the whole call, opt-in jittered retry, and an address pinned before connecting.

rules.title: `Core\Http\Client` has no spelling for "wait forever": every bound is a `Duration`, an omitted one inherits `[http.client]`, and expiry throws `TimeoutError`
rules.diverges: curl defaults to no timeout and `file_get_contents` to `default_socket_timeout`'s sixty seconds; here there is no `null`, no `0` and no option that means unbounded, so a long call names its own `deadline`

rules.title: An outbound request carries at most one body, named by which of four flat keys it is written under, and a second key or a body on `get` is a compile-time diagnostic
rules.diverges: curl takes `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` as a string, an array or a file handle and infers the encoding from which one it got; here the key names what is sent, two keys are refused before the program runs, and a `Part::file` streams from disk rather than being held whole

rules.title: One `deadline` covers the whole call: the connection, every redirect hop, every retry attempt and every backoff between them
rules.diverges: curl's `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` bounds one transfer, so three attempts at five seconds is a fifteen-second call; here the stated number is the bound on everything

rules.title: `deadline` ends at the head of a streamed reply, its body runs under `idle` and `maxDuration`, and the body is read one way, once
rules.diverges: a PHP stream has `default_socket_timeout` and nothing that bounds how long a body may take; here a streamed body has two finite bounds it cannot be without, and reading it twice throws

rules.title: Retry is opt-in, exponential with full jitter that cannot be turned off, and retries only a connection failure, a timeout, `429`, `502`, `503` and `504`
rules.diverges: PHP's clients have no retry, so every application writes its own loop; here it is three flat options, the jitter is not configurable, and a `Retry-After` header replaces the computed wait

rules.title: A `POST` or `PATCH` is not retried without `retryIdempotencyKey`, and at an ordinary call site the missing key is a compile-time diagnostic
rules.diverges: a retried `POST` in PHP does whatever the loop the developer wrote does, including charging a card twice; here the missing key is a red squiggle before the program runs

rules.title: `Core\Http::allowUrl` resolves, checks and pins: it answers a `Target` carrying the URL and every approved address, and the connection is made to one of them
rules.diverges: `file_get_contents($userUrl)` and `curl_setopt(CURLOPT_URL, $userUrl)` are a compile-time diagnostic, and the laundered value is a `Target` the program cannot read an address back out of, not a string

rules.title: Every address a name resolves to is checked, one denied refuses the host, and the call falls back across the approved set without ever resolving twice
rules.diverges: curl tries every address a name answers and checks none of them; here each is checked before any is tried, one denied refuses the whole host, and the lookup runs off the core

rules.title: `connectTo` names an outbound call's address only where `net.connect_to` names the host, and the address policy and the certificate's host check still apply
rules.diverges: `CURLOPT_RESOLVE` takes any host-to-address mapping a script writes; here the host must be granted, the address is judged by the same policy a resolved one is, and the certificate is still checked against the URL's host

rules.title: Redirects are not followed by default; when enabled every hop is re-checked and re-pinned, a denied hop fails the request, and a retry never re-resolves
rules.diverges: curl's `FOLLOWLOCATION` is off by default too, but a hop it follows is never checked against anything; here each hop passes the same policy the first URL did and a denied one fails the call rather than being dropped from the chain

rules.title: A redirect from `https` to `http` needs `net.downgrade` for its host and `redirectToHttp` at the call; a plain `http` URL asked for directly stays allowed
rules.diverges: curl follows a hop from `https` to `http` silently, so one `Location` header strips a call's TLS; here it needs a grant and a call-site option, and the refusal names the grant

rules.title: A redirect hop to another origin carries none of the caller's own headers, the three named credentials and every `secret` value among them
rules.diverges: an `Authorization` header set in a stream context is re-sent to whatever host a `Location` names; here a hop to another origin carries no header the program wrote, that one and every `secret` value included

rules.title: An outbound connection is pooled per core under a key carrying everything the check approved, and returns to the pool only after a reply read to the end under known framing
rules.diverges: curl reuses a connection keyed on host and port inside one handle, and PHP's stream functions reuse nothing; here the key carries the pinned address, the client identity and the call's TLS policy, so reuse cannot widen what a check approved

rules.title: `[http.client.proxy]` is the only way an outbound call is proxied: `System` class, written by the operator, and never a call option or an environment variable
rules.diverges: curl and PHP's stream wrappers take a proxy from `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY` in the environment, or per handle from `CURLOPT_PROXY`; here it is one root-owned block, no environment variable is read, and no program-side spelling exists

rules.title: `resolve` is mandatory: `local` tunnels to the address Novis approved and keeps the pin, `proxy` narrows the policy to the URL's text and warns at every boot
rules.diverges: curl hands the proxy the destination's host name in every case, having no approved address to hand it; here that is one of two written answers, the other tunnels to the address the check approved, and the one that gives up the pin is announced at every boot

rules.title: `[http.client.tls]` is the operator's alone: the bundled roots unless files are named, TLS 1.2 unless the floor is raised, and no key log in `production`
rules.diverges: `curl.cainfo` and `openssl.cafile` are `ini` settings a script can widen with `ini_set`; here the three keys are `System` class and no code-side spelling for any of them exists

rules.title: `Response::tls()` reports the session a reply arrived over — version, cipher, whether the peer was verified, and its chain — and is `null` when there was none
rules.diverges: `curl_getinfo` answers a flat array of thirty-odd keys mixing timings, sizes and TLS facts; here the session is an object read through members and the timings are the trace's

rules.title: A WebSocket is opened by `Core\Http\Client::openSocket` under every rule an outbound call obeys, `ws` and `wss` serve that row alone, and a socket is never pooled
rules.diverges: there is no outbound WebSocket in PHP's standard library at all — `ext-sockets` and a userland client are what a program reaches for, and neither passes an address policy

rules.title: An outbound socket is charged to the task that opened it and closed with `1001` when that task ends, and it is never a root isolate
`idle`, `maxDuration`, `maxMessage` and `sendTimeout` bound every outbound socket, each inherits a finite default, and none has an unbounded spelling

sections.title: Containment
sections.blurb: Nothing a request can send terminates a worker. Four bounded tiers, a watchdog that sheds rather than kills, and one stated residue.

rules.title: Nothing a request can send terminates or wedges a worker: its blast radius is bounded at four named tiers, and the residue is one stated fault class
rules.diverges: there is no worker process per request to die and be respawned; a request is contained in-process and the process boundary is reserved for one named residue

rules.title: A worker task's root is wrapped in `catch_unwind`: a panic beneath a request fails that request, and one outside any request retires the worker
Every engine-side recursive descent over request data carries a depth counter and refuses past it, with a limit per decoder and `512` for JSON
A helper whose runtime scales with its input polls the request's deadline flag through a bounded-loop combinator, or bounds its input instead
rules.diverges: `max_execution_time` fires between statements; here a deadline also reaches inside one `Core` call over a large value, and reaches it by a flag rather than a clock

rules.title: No path reaches `abort()`: nothing on a teardown path panics, teardown is iterative, and an allocation sized by request data is fallible
A core is never blocked on a syscall: filesystem calls, name resolution and waiting on a child go to a blocking pool bounded at twice the core count
A watchdog reads the in-flight deadline each worker already keeps, and reports a core whose oldest deadline is past by a margin
A reported core stops accepting and `max_in_flight` counts its share as unavailable; a wedged worker is never killed in-process
A client that goes away cancels its request tree at the next safepoint; nothing is waited out
rules.diverges: PHP-FPM learns of a closed tab at the script's next write and holds the worker until `max_execution_time`; here the connection's drop is an event, the tree is cancelled and no worker was ever held

rules.title: Every timeout, deadline and backoff in the engine is computed on a monotonic clock
The floor cannot fill the disk it writes to: a file target rotates under a retention bound, repeats coalesce into one record with a count, and a cache write failure compiles in memory
A page holding generated code is writable while written and executable only after being made read-only
A memory-safety fault in `unsafe` code or a miscompile is the one residue: the process dies, the supervisor restarts it, and the answer is frequency, not a boundary
rules.diverges: there is no per-request worker process to absorb an engine crash; a fault of this class loses every request in flight and is answered by a restart in about a cold start

sections.title: Declaring a route
sections.blurb: A route is an attribute compiled into a table. Structural precedence, captures that narrow to closed sets, and no wildcard verb.

rules.title: A route is a `#[Route]` compiled into the unit's table, and its three runtime bugs are compile errors
rules.diverges: there is no runtime registry and no routes file — a `$router->get(...)` call has no counterpart, and a duplicate route, an unbound placeholder or a stale link name fails the build rather than a request

rules.title: `#[Route]` is `{path, method, name?}` on a method, recognized by name and never by shape
rules.diverges: the attribute is read while compiling rather than by a reflection scan at boot, a route's name is never derived from the class and method, and there is no class-level prefix attribute

rules.title: A path is literal segments and three capture forms, each capture a whole segment naming a parameter
rules.diverges: `{name}` rather than `:name`, a capture is always a whole segment so `/u{id}` and `/{id}.json` are refused rather than partially matched, and there is no inline constraint — the parameter's type is the constraint

rules.title: There is no wildcard verb: `method` is required, singular, and one case of a closed enum
rules.diverges: `Route::any()` and `methods: ['*']` have no spelling — each verb a route answers is its own `#[Route]` line, because `Allow:` and the CSRF classification read the exact set

rules.title: Precedence is structural — a literal beats a capture beats an optional beats a catch-all — never declaration order
rules.diverges: a routes file is not read top to bottom — first-match-wins does not exist, so moving a declaration between files cannot change which route answers

rules.title: A capture narrows to a closed set with a literal-union or enum-subset type, never with a regex
rules.diverges: there is no `->where('lang', 'en|de|fr')`; the constraint is the parameter's type, and a regex on a route is refused outright

rules.title: An enum capture is spelled by a written backing value, and by its case name when the value was counted
rules.diverges: there is no backed-versus-pure split to route on — every enum is integer-backed, so what decides the spelling is whether the value was written

rules.title: `{name?}` captures one trailing segment or none, and its parameter's default is what makes the absent case well-typed
rules.diverges: an optional segment is declared by the parameter's default, not by a second route or an optional regex group, and `/posts/` does not match `/posts/{page?}`

rules.title: A `#[Query]` parameter is declared with a capture's type list, and a default is what makes it optional
rules.diverges: a query key is declared on the handler's parameter with a type, matched nominally as `Core\Query`, rather than read out of `$_GET` and validated by hand

rules.title: A query value that fails to convert is a `400`, where a path capture that fails is a `404`
rules.diverges: a bad query value is refused with a 400 before the handler sees it, instead of arriving as a string the handler casts and checks

rules.title: One method's repeated routes may share a `name` only when they share a `path`; every other duplicate name is a compile error
rules.diverges: a framework's `methods: ['POST', 'PUT']` on one named route becomes one `#[Route]` line per verb, each carrying the same `name` and the same `path`

rules.title: A shared name is one `url()` target, one `Match::name` for every verb, and one `operationId` per verb
rules.diverges: the generated `operationId` is the route name, suffixed with the lowercased verb only where two operations share it — never a counter

sections.title: Matching, not dispatching
sections.blurb: The router stops at a name and typed parameters. It carries nothing invocable, and the server dispatches none of it.

rules.title: The router stops at matching: a match is a name and typed parameters, and nothing here dispatches
rules.diverges: no framework router's dispatch is here — no controller base class, no middleware, no return-value-to-response rule, no `HEAD`-implies-`GET` or trailing-slash normalisation; the program or its framework writes the `switch`

rules.title: A match carries a name and typed parameters and nothing invocable, and typed `callable` would not change that
rules.diverges: there is no `$route->getCallable()`; the handler is reached by a `switch` the framework generates or the application writes

rules.title: A request is matched once, before any application code runs, and `Core\Request::route()` is that match
rules.diverges: the match is made by the server and read off the request, not by a framework kernel in userland that matches and then calls the controller

rules.title: The server's match dispatches nothing, and a request the table does not claim is served by the program
rules.diverges: a matched route never calls anything; the program or the framework dispatches, and a `null` route is a fact the program reads rather than a 404 anything sends

rules.title: A missing path and a refused verb are different answers, and `methodsFor` is what tells them apart
rules.diverges: a wrong verb on a known path is a 405 with an `Allow:` list asked of the table, rather than the 404 a hand-rolled dispatch falls into

rules.title: `Core\Request::mount()` answers the prefix the door stripped and the tainted host captures, and it is never `null`
rules.diverges: the deployment prefix is never derived from `REQUEST_URI` or `SCRIPT_NAME`; the server hands it over, and a tenant is a mount capture rather than a `host` field on the route

sections.title: Links and the API document
sections.blurb: Link building is checked against the compiled table, and the OpenAPI document is generated from that same table while compiling.

rules.title: `Core\Router::url` is a launderer whose literal name and `$params` are checked against the compiled table
rules.diverges: a link is built from the route's name and checked while compiling, never assembled by hand — a renamed route fails the build at every stale `url()` rather than in a sent email

rules.title: A link carries the mount prefix the request arrived under, so one table serves at any mount
rules.diverges: a link is never the declared path concatenated by hand, because the path a route is declared against is the mount-stripped one and the prefix is known only where the request is

rules.title: A `url()` key that is not a capture becomes a percent-encoded query string, and one that is neither a capture nor a declared `#[Query]` parameter does not compile
rules.diverges: the query string is built by the same member that builds the path, and `url(...) . '?page=' . $n` is the concatenation the launderer exists to prevent

rules.title: `urlAbsolute` prepends a configured origin and never one sniffed from a request header
rules.diverges: there is no base URL derived from `$_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']`; an absolute link comes from a configured origin or the call throws

rules.title: An origin is declared per mount with `[app] origin` as the fallback, a request cannot set it, and a mount that calls `urlAbsolute` without one is a boot error
rules.diverges: a multi-tenant deployment configures one origin line with a capture in it rather than computing a base URL per request

rules.title: The table is built by the program enumeration, and a program with no `#[Route]` builds none and pays nothing
rules.diverges: there is no route cache to warm or to go stale — the scan is compile-time work keyed and invalidated with the compiled unit

rules.title: The API document is generated from the route table while compiling, so it cannot drift from the code
rules.diverges: there is no hand-written or annotation-scanned OpenAPI file to keep in sync — the document is a build output of the route table, and a program with no `#[Route]` produces none

rules.title: `nvs build --openapi` writes OpenAPI 3.1 as a build artifact, and two builds of one source are byte-identical
rules.diverges: no `/openapi.json` endpoint the running server assembles — the document is written at build time and served as a file, and there is no 3.0 or Swagger 2 output

rules.title: `nvs api diff` classifies every change as breaking, additive or cosmetic, and exits non-zero on a breaking one
rules.diverges: a broken client contract is a failed build rather than a reviewer's judgement, and there is no suppression to wave one through

rules.title: A `#[Route]` missing its `path` gets a quick fix that offers a derived one, and nothing derives a path on its own
rules.diverges: no convention routing — a class rename never moves a URL, because the derived path is inserted as source text once and is ordinary text from then on

sections.title: The file and the tree
sections.blurb: It is TOML, it is a deployment file rather than a project manifest, and a host with no file at all is fully configured.

rules.title: The configuration file is `nvs.toml`, and it is TOML
rules.diverges: there is no INI dialect: the file is TOML, its name is `nvs.toml`, and no `php.ini` carries over under any syntax because the directive set shares almost no key with it

rules.title: A size or a duration is a quoted string carrying its suffix, a count is an integer, and `false` removes a ceiling
rules.diverges: `memory_limit = 128M` becomes `memory = "128M"` — quoted, because the value is typed and the suffix is part of it — and `-1` for no limit becomes `false`

rules.title: A list is a TOML array, a repeated record is an array of tables, and a dotted key is table nesting
rules.diverges: no comma-joined or `PATH`-joined strings: a list of roots is `["/a", "/b", "C:\\srv"]`, which is what makes a Windows absolute path spellable at all

rules.title: A duplicate key is an error, and so is an unknown one — per file
rules.diverges: `php.ini` silently takes the last of two copies of a key and ignores one it does not recognise; both refuse the boot here, naming the line

rules.title: The block roster is closed, and each block's directives are argued by the rule that adds it
`nvs.toml` is a deployment file, never a project manifest, and it is never found by walking up
rules.diverges: there is no `.user.ini` or `.htaccess` discovered beside the code — the file is read from one directory the operator chose, and it holds no source-tree state

rules.title: The root of the tree is every `--config` in order, else `./nvs.toml`, else the shipped defaults
rules.diverges: there is no search path, no `PHPRC` and no compiled-in location: a `--config` list, else `./nvs.toml` in exactly the working directory, else the shipped defaults

rules.title: A host with no configuration file runs on the shipped defaults, which are a complete configuration and not an error
rules.diverges: a host without a `php.ini` runs on PHP's built-in defaults, which allow nearly everything; the shipped defaults here deny every capability and start in `production`

rules.title: The resolved root is canonicalized once at boot, announced with every file it reached, and re-read from that stored path on reload

sections.title: Includes, ownership and secrets
sections.blurb: One ordered stream where later wins and every override is recorded — over files nobody but the runtime account may write.

rules.title: `[[include]]` takes a `path` or a `dir`, never both and never neither, and a `dir` is not a glob
rules.diverges: PHP's `--with-config-file-scan-dir` reads a directory in an order the build chose; here a `dir` include is every `*.toml` directly inside it, ascending by filename, written in the file itself

rules.title: An include cycle is refused with the chain named, and nesting past eight is refused as depth
The tree is one ordered stream, a later assignment wins, and every override is recorded with both origins
rules.diverges: an include may override the file that pulled it in — the base-plus-local shape — but only because the override is reported; nothing is shadowed silently the way a later `php.ini` line shadows an earlier one

rules.title: A value array is replaced wholesale by a later file; `[[table]]` entries accumulate across the tree
A relative path resolves against the directory of the file it is written in; a command-line path against the working directory
rules.diverges: a relative path in `php.ini` resolves against whatever the process's working directory happens to be; here it resolves against the file that wrote it, so a config directory survives being copied whole

rules.title: Any file in the tree may set any directive, `System` class included
rules.diverges: there is no `PHP_INI_SYSTEM` versus `PHP_INI_PERDIR` split between files: an included file clears the same ownership bar as the root file and may grant a capability, set `[limits.hard]` or add an `[[extension]]`

rules.title: Every file the configuration reads, and its directory, must be owned by the runtime account or root and writable by nobody else
rules.diverges: PHP reads `php.ini` and `.user.ini` whatever their owner and mode; a config file or its directory that any other account can write refuses the boot, on Unix by mode and on Windows by effective DACL rights

rules.title: The ownership check runs on `nvs serve` and on reload; `nvs run`, `config check` and `config dump` read without it, and an unchecked file can grant nothing
`optional = true` covers absence and nothing else, and an absent include is checked at the directory that would hold it
A secret directive has a `_file` sibling, exactly one of the pair is set, and the file's whole content is the value
rules.diverges: a credential arrives as a file — `password_file = "/run/secrets/db_password"` — with one trailing newline stripped and nothing else trimmed, rather than inline in the file or interpolated from the environment

rules.title: A secret file another account can write refuses the boot; one another account can read only warns

sections.title: Changeability classes
sections.blurb: The file states defaults, not ceilings. Three classes decide what a running request may change, and a refusal is never a clamp.

rules.title: The boot path and `Core\Config::set` parse a value through one implementation
The configuration is one immutable snapshot a request clones at start, and a reload replaces it whole after validating everything
rules.diverges: nothing is re-read on the request path — no `.user.ini` scan, no per-directory override — and a reload that fails leaves the old configuration serving rather than half of each

rules.title: `nvs.toml` states defaults, not ceilings, and every directive carries one of three changeability classes
rules.diverges: `ini_set` may widen `memory_limit` here too, but only up to a ceiling the file states in its own block, and a `System` directive has no `ini_set` at all

rules.title: A CLI flag that sets a directive is one of a closed list, wins over every file, and there is no `--set`
rules.diverges: there is no `php -d key=value`: argv is world-readable and would be a second spelling of the whole format, so only the flags a rule introduces by name reach a directive

rules.title: Reloadability is a second registry field, `Reload` or `Boot`, orthogonal to the changeability class
rules.diverges: there is no `PHP_INI_SYSTEM` bundle meaning both "the file only" and "read once at boot"; the two questions are two fields

rules.title: A ceiling is a `System` directive with the default's key name, and `false` removes it
rules.diverges: there is no `-1` meaning unlimited; a ceiling is removed with `false` in a root-owned block, and never from a script — and PHP's one `max_execution_time`, CPU time on Linux and elapsed time on Windows, is two keys: `cpu_time` and `wall_time`

rules.title: A directive is `System` when changing it from inside a request would affect something other than that request, and that is all `System` means
Every runtime change lives in the request's own overlay and dies with the request
rules.diverges: an `ini_set` never outlives the request even under a long-running process, and no other request can observe it

rules.title: A refused `Core\Config::set` returns `false` and leaves the value unchanged; it is never clamped
rules.diverges: `false` is what PHP returns too, but a value above the ceiling is refused whole rather than run at some other number

rules.title: `ini_set` is `Core\Config::set`, and the whole family crosses as strings
rules.diverges: `ini_set`, `ini_get`, `ini_restore` and `ini_get_all` are static members of `Core\Config`, a refused set answers `false` and moves nothing, and an accepted one is request-local

sections.title: Reloading and control
sections.blurb: An edit reaches the next request without a restart, and the running process is controlled over one local socket and no network surface.

rules.title: A source change reaches the next request in every mode: every file a program reached is checked in the background, and a change is compiled whole from a quiet tree before one pointer swap
rules.diverges: `opcache.validate_timestamps` shape, but the check runs in the background rather than in a request, the cache key is the program's content rather than a file's path, so a stale `mtime` never serves stale code, and there is no `opcache_reset()` and no `validate_timestamps=0`

rules.title: A file is resolved once per isolate, so an edit is invisible to a request already running
A revalidated file that no longer compiles fails the requests that resolve it afterwards, loudly, and the last good version is never served in its place
rules.diverges: the same behaviour as `validate_timestamps`, chosen over the more forgiving keep-serving policy some caches adopt

rules.title: A reload reports what it applied, names every changed `Boot` key it could not apply, and counts the units it invalidated
rules.diverges: a changed listen address is named in the reply rather than silently ignored until the next restart

rules.title: The server is controlled over one local socket whose owner and mode are the authentication, and `nvs ctl` is its client
rules.diverges: there is no `SIGUSR2`, no `php-fpm reload` and no signal at all; the operator speaks HTTP to a local socket and gets a report back

rules.title: There is no network-reachable control surface, in either direction of configuration
`nvs ctl config` reports what the running process actually holds, including an optional include that appeared after boot
`nvs config check` and `nvs config dump` resolve the tree with no server, and `dump --origin` names where every value came from
rules.diverges: `php --ini` names the files read and `phpinfo()` prints values from inside a request; here one offline command validates the whole tree in CI and names, per key, the file and line that set it and the one it overrode

sections.title: Run modes
sections.blurb: Exactly two, defaulting to production, selected by the file or a flag and never by an environment variable.

rules.title: A run mode is one of exactly two closed values, and with nothing configured it is `production`
rules.diverges: there is no `php.ini-development`/`php.ini-production` pair to copy and no `APP_ENV`; staging is `production` with different configuration, not a third value

rules.title: The mode a server starts in comes from `nvs.toml` or from `nvs serve --mode=`, and the flag is the last word
No environment variable selects the run mode — not `NVS_MODE`, not `APP_ENV`, not `NODE_ENV`
rules.diverges: `APP_ENV` and its kind are ordinary `Core\Env::get` values with no effect on the runtime; the operator's switch is a reload of the root-owned file

rules.title: A mode is a shorthand for the defaults of five `Runtime` directives, and governs nothing else
rules.diverges: "what does development mode change?" has a closed, printable answer, which no `APP_ENV` or `NODE_ENV` convention can give

rules.title: A mode also selects three startup defaults, chosen when a configuration is published, never re-derived by a mode flip, and never flippable from code
A program may read the mode and may flip it for its own request, bounded by a `System` ceiling
rules.diverges: a script can turn development defaults on for itself only where the operator opened a ceiling, and the flip never reaches another request

sections.title: Application blocks
sections.blurb: An application is its entry file path. A mount routes; an `[[app]]` block sets policy, bounded by the global ceiling.

rules.title: An application is its entry file path, and an `[[app]]` block is keyed on a `root` directory or one `entry` file
rules.diverges: a per-directory `php.ini`, a `.user.ini` or a PHP-FPM pool keys on a directory the web server chose; an `[[app]]` block keys on the entry file's own path, so `nvs run` has the same identity as a served request

rules.title: Both sides of an `[[app]]` match are canonicalized first, and a key naming nothing examinable refuses the boot
`origin` and `mode` sit on the `[[app]]` block itself, and there is no global `[app]` table
Every matching `[[app]]` block applies, least-specific `root` first, and two blocks on one canonical path are a duplicate
rules.diverges: PHP applies the nearest `.user.ini` and stops; here a host-wide block and an application's own block compose, the narrower one winning only the keys it states

rules.title: An `[[app]]` block may widen a limit or grant a capability up to the global ceiling, and may only lower its own ceiling
rules.diverges: a per-directory `php.ini` can only move what `PHP_INI_PERDIR` allows; an `[[app]]` block sets any `[app.limits]` value up to `[limits.hard]` and grants a capability the global block withholds, so the root file denies and each application states what it needs

rules.title: A `[[server.mount]]` routes and carries no `mode`; an `[[app]]` block sets policy

sections.title: Scheduled work
sections.blurb: A config block, not a runtime API: five cron fields, a mandatory scope, a lease across a fleet, and a missed fire that stays missed.

rules.title: Scheduled work is a `[[schedule]]` entry firing a `spawn script`, checked at boot, with no runtime API
rules.diverges: there is no crontab line and no scheduler API — a job, its cadence and its concurrency policy are an entry in `nvs.toml`, refused at boot when it cannot be armed

rules.title: `cron` is five-field POSIX plus five named shorthands, parsed at boot with the line named
rules.diverges: a seconds field or Quartz's `L`/`W`/`#`/`?` is refused at boot rather than accepted by whichever cron the host happens to run

rules.title: `scope` is mandatory with no default, and `fleet` with no shared store refuses to boot
rules.diverges: the `flock`-and-hope guard a PHP deployment adds per cron job is one required word per entry, and forgetting it is a boot error rather than four copies of a nightly run

rules.title: Every `[[schedule]]` key is `System`, and not even `RuntimeTighten` reaches one
rules.diverges: no `ini_set` or `.user.ini` can add, remove or retime a job — a request cannot touch the schedule at all

rules.title: An entry's `limits` and `grants` narrow the deployment's, and can never widen them
A scheduled run is a root isolate that spends a root's budget, and only `nvs serve` fires one
rules.diverges: a cron-invoked `php` process gets no limits, no capability narrowing and no place to report but a mail spool; a scheduled run gets the deployment's `[limits]`, its `[capabilities]` and the escalation ladder because it is an ordinary isolate

rules.title: A `fleet` entry fires once per interval across the deployment under a lease in the shared store — at most once, never exactly once
`overlap` is `skip` by default, `queue` holds exactly one pending run, and `kill` cancels before it starts
A missed fire is never caught up, `timezone` defaults to UTC, and a DST gap or repeat fires exactly once
rules.diverges: there is no ambient timezone to fall back on and no anacron-style replay — the interval a host slept through is logged as skipped, not run late

sections.title: Stores, sockets and the compiled-unit cache
sections.blurb: Where a Unix socket may be written, why the extension set is in every cache key, and which opcache directives an operator alone owns.

rules.title: A store an operator configured is authorized by the configuring — `cache.shared` is the grant, unscoped, and asks no address
rules.diverges: a Redis on loopback needs one grant naming the store, not a host allow-list plus an exception for the loopback range the store lives in

rules.title: A Unix socket is admitted in `[cache.shared] url` and `[db.<name>] host`, and refused from any program-supplied endpoint
rules.diverges: `Redis::connect('/run/redis.sock')` and a socket path in a DSN a program builds are refused — the path has to be in root-owned configuration

rules.title: A socket is `unix:` where the key is a URL and a bare absolute path where the key is a host
rules.diverges: `redis://`, `rediss://` and `unix:` are the only schemes `[cache.shared] url` reads — a credential is `[cache.shared] password` rather than userinfo, and a database index is `[cache.shared] database` rather than a path on the URL

rules.title: A Unix spelling on a build with no `AF_UNIX` transport is refused at boot, never read as loopback TCP
A program-supplied socket path needs `net.local`, a path-scoped grant carrying no address policy and governing both ends
The extension set is folded into one `env_hash` that both compiled-unit cache keys carry, so an extension change is an ordinary cache miss
`opcache.validate`, its rate cap and `opcache.settle` are `System`, `validate` has no `never`, and `settle`'s startup default is chosen by the run mode
rules.diverges: `opcache.validate_timestamps` and `revalidate_freq` are `PHP_INI_ALL` in PHP; here no request may touch either, and there is no value that turns checking off

rules.title: The five `opcache.file_cache*` directives are `System`-class, because where compiled code is read from is a code-injection primitive
rules.diverges: `opcache.file_cache` and `opcache.file_cache_dir` cannot be moved by `ini_set` or `.user.ini`; only the root-owned file sets them

rules.title: The update-check and telemetry endpoints are compiled-in defaults overridable by `NVS_UPDATE_URL` and `NVS_TELEMETRY_URL`

sections.title: The compiled-unit cache
sections.blurb: One immutable file addressed by its content and environment, verified whole before a page becomes executable.

rules.title: A compiled unit is one immutable file whose address is its content and its environment
rules.diverges: opcache's file cache is keyed by path and revalidated by timestamp; an artifact here is keyed by the source's digest and the environment's, so a file built for another machine, compiler or extension set is never opened at all

rules.title: An artifact is a self-describing header over one relocatable object, and it carries no class metadata
A compiled-unit cache entry is read into memory, never mapped
A warm hit skips codegen and nothing else, and it must beat the compile it replaces
An artifact is hashed in full where it lies, then placed, relocated and only then made executable
The checksum answers corruption; a cache directory another account can write is refused at startup
rules.diverges: opcache.file_cache_dir is taken as written; a directory that is world-writable or not owned by the runtime's own account refuses the process rather than the entry

rules.title: A bad cache entry is a miss the script never sees, and only a corrupt one is deleted
A writer publishes by one atomic rename, and a path that already exists wins
Eviction rides the cold miss at a configured probability, and a warm hit pays nothing for it
`nvs cache gc` and `nvs cache clear` are the operator's deterministic alternative to the roll
A unit's cache key covers every autoload path it probed, misses included, and every directory a discovery query listed
rules.diverges: OPcache revalidates the files it compiled; here adding a file that shadows an already-resolved name, or a module nothing references yet, invalidates the unit although no hashed file changed

rules.title: A compiled extension module is cached in the same store, under the same key, header and verify shape

sections.title: Single-file builds
sections.blurb: A bundle is source appended to a copy of the host binary, found by a footer, carrying a notice generated from the dependency graph.

rules.title: `nvs build --compile` appends a program to a copy of the `nvs` binary, and rebundling is running it again
rules.diverges: there is no `.phar` and no archive format: the shipped file is the runtime itself with the source appended, and it is remade by its author rather than updated in place

rules.title: A bundle's payload is source, as a flat file list with no archive and no compression
rules.diverges: a `.phar` can be stripped or compressed; a bundle's source is embedded byte for byte and is recoverable by anyone who looks

rules.title: Inside a closed-world target every `require` resolves at build time, and one that cannot fails the build
rules.diverges: an `include` whose path is computed at run time has no filesystem to fall back on inside a bundle, so the build refuses it instead of the run failing on the user's machine

rules.title: A bundle is recognised by a footer the host reads before it parses one argument
`nvs build --compile` packages what is already resolved on disk and fetches no dependency
rules.diverges: there is no `composer install` step inside the bundler: resolving dependencies and packaging them are two commands that compose, not one

rules.title: A `.nvsx` the program depends on is embedded as one opaque entry of the same flat list
A macOS bundle is ad-hoc signed by the build command; PE and ELF need no step
A build records its target, host, profile, compiler, commit and the commit's own date, and never a build date
`nvs --help` opens with the README's own title and the version, commit and commit date of the build answering
`nvs.exe` carries the logo as its icon and the manifest's facts as its version information, and a debug build carries its own icon
The third-party notice is generated from the dependency graph, fails closed, and is never written by hand
The notice and Novis's own license are compiled into the binary from the same tree
No flag on `nvs` is inherited from PHP; `-h` and `-V` are the Unix baseline and `-o` the only short flag Novis declares
rules.diverges: `php` carries `-i`, `-a`, `-r`, `-f` and a lowercase `-v`; `nvs` inherits none of them, spells every operation as a subcommand, and declares exactly one short flag of its own

rules.title: A doc comment clap renders is written for the person reading `--help`, and cites nothing they cannot open
rules.diverges: `php --help` lists flags the manual explains elsewhere; `nvs --help` is the explanation, and it names no repository document, no decision record and no file extension the binary does not act on

rules.title: `nvs info` is the one call for build, host and licensing facts, and the one spelling of it
rules.diverges: `php -i` prints ini settings and the request's own server variables; `nvs info` reports the build, the host and the licences, never per-request state, and it is spelled one way

sections.title: Packages
sections.blurb: A package is its digest, reached by an ordinary autoload line, and nothing in one runs before your program does.

rules.title: A package name is `vendor/name`, lowercase ASCII compared exactly, and `nvs` is reserved for first-party packages
rules.diverges: Composer lowercases and compares names case-insensitively; here a name is compared exactly so that one which resolves on one operating system resolves on all three

rules.title: A package is an immutable source archive whose identity is its BLAKE3 digest
rules.diverges: a Composer dependency is a name that resolves to whatever the registry serves today; here two archives with the same digest are the same package and two with different digests are different packages whatever they call themselves

rules.title: `package.toml` is read by the `nvs` CLI, never by the runtime and never by name resolution
rules.diverges: composer.json drives the autoloader; here a populated `vendor/` resolves every name identically whether the manifest is present, absent or malformed

rules.title: Every file in a fetched package declares a namespace under the prefix its manifest claims, and two packages claiming one prefix is a fetch error naming both
rules.diverges: a Composer package may declare any PSR-4 prefix, including the application's; here a package file declaring `namespace App;` to reach the application's grants fails to compile

rules.title: A fetched package is reached by an ordinary `autoload` line in a committed, generated `vendor/packages.nvs`
rules.diverges: there is no `vendor/autoload.php` classmap or loader to `require`; the generated file holds declarations the compiler resolves like any other source

rules.title: Nothing in a package runs before your program does
rules.diverges: Composer's `scripts` (`post-install-cmd` and friends) and plugins execute at install time; here there is no hook, build step, macro or code generation of any kind

rules.title: A package ships no `nvs.toml`, and none of its `require` or `autoload` paths reaches outside its own directory
rules.diverges: a Composer package's files may `require` anything the process can read; here a `..`, an absolute path or a symlink that leaves the package is a compile error

rules.title: Resolution selects the highest minimum any package asked for, and nothing upgrades itself
rules.diverges: there are no version ranges and no solver, so `^1.4` and "your requirements could not be resolved" both cease to exist; a version arrives only because somebody named it

rules.title: `package.lock` records every package's digest, a mismatch is a hard error, and `--locked` fetches nothing the lock does not name
rules.diverges: composer.lock pins a version and a `dist` URL; here the lock pins bytes, and a vendored tree is re-checked against it on every build rather than trusted once

rules.title: A git dependency pins an exact commit, and only the root application may declare one
rules.diverges: a `vcs` repository in composer.json may name a branch and is honoured anywhere in the graph; here a git source names a commit and is refused below the root, at publish and at fetch

sections.title: The registry and the version contract
sections.blurb: An append-only transparency log, retraction rather than deletion, and a ladder a dependency break goes down before it is forwarded.

rules.title: The registry publishes an append-only transparency log, and a client verifies inclusion and consistency before using an artifact
rules.diverges: Packagist can serve one client different bytes than another with nothing to show for it; here a registry that does so must fork a signed log, which the next consistency check reports

rules.title: `nvs publish` uploads a clean-checkout archive, and the registry never overwrites a published `name@version`
rules.diverges: a Packagist release is whatever tag the repository points at and can be moved; here a published version is immutable and is in the transparency log before it is downloadable

rules.title: A known-bad version is retracted, never deleted, and `nvs audit` names the minimum bump that clears it
rules.diverges: Packagist lets a publisher delete a release, which breaks every lockfile naming it; here the bytes stay fetchable forever and only selection refuses them

rules.title: A package that breaks its API publishes under a new name carrying `supersedes`
rules.diverges: `2.0.0` of the same name is how Composer ships a break; here the break is `acme/http2`, and the old and new package coexist in one graph without conflict

rules.title: Until 0.1.0 ships any dependency updates at any time, and the version contract starts with the commit that tags 0.1.0
A version number describes the enumerated surface, and the Rust crate APIs, the artifact cache, diagnostic prose and MSRV carry no promise
One `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` for the whole workspace, and below 1.0 the breaking slot moves left
rules.diverges: PHP numbers a runtime that programs then target; here `nvs --version` is the language version, and `0.MINOR` rather than `MAJOR` is what carries a break until 1.0

rules.title: A change a dependency forced ships as a patch, a minor or a major by who can see it, never by how big the diff was
A dependency break that a program author could see goes down a seven-step ladder, and shipping it is the last step
rules.diverges: PHP's own minors have broken running applications, and a Composer library forwards its dependencies' breaks as its own; here a dependency-forced break reaches a program author only after adapting, wrapping, compensating, holding, vendoring and replacing have all been tried

rules.title: A forced user-facing break survives one minor release as a warning naming its replacement, and is removed in the next major
rules.diverges: PHP's deprecation notices are runtime `E_DEPRECATED` output a production `error_reporting` hides; here the warning is the compiler's, and a warning that does not name the replacement is not a deprecation

rules.title: A dependency move never fixes a guard test by editing its threshold, and it regenerates the attribution file in the same commit
Each dependency bump is its own commit, classified in its message
Being current has a schedule, a stale dependency is a defect, and a human fires every pass — never an agent, cron or CI
rules.diverges: a PHP shop's `composer update` and the runtime's own upgrade are separate projects on nobody's calendar; here the toolchain, every crate, CI actions and the PHP oracle move on one dated cadence

sections.title: Extensions
sections.blurb: A third-party extension is a sandboxed WebAssembly component: fresh per request, no ambient authority, statically typed at the call.

rules.title: A third-party extension is a sandboxed WebAssembly component, never a shared library loaded with `dlopen`
rules.diverges: there is no `extension=` line and no `.so`; an extension is one portable `.nvsx` that cannot address host memory, and nothing loads native code at runtime

rules.title: Library and extension code sits at one of three tiers: built-in, sandboxed component, or statically linked native
The image and intl components are built into every `nvs` binary, sandboxed, and always present under `Novis\`
The prebuilt libwebp wasm library is committed beside its source hash, and CI rebuilds it and fails on a difference
A `.nvsx` is a single WebAssembly component whose manifest is an `nvs.manifest` custom section
rules.diverges: a PHP extension is a per-platform binary registered by an ini line; an `.nvsx` is one file for every platform and carries its own declarations inside it

rules.title: An extension package may carry Novis source beside its `.nvsx`, under one namespace, and the component's manifest registers exactly one class
rules.diverges: a Composer package is source only and a PHP extension is a binary only; an extension package here is both, and the builder a program names is ordinary Novis source

rules.title: An extension loads only from an `[[extension]]` entry in the root-owned `nvs.toml`, pinned by its `sha256`
rules.diverges: `extension=` in a `php.ini` names a file; an `[[extension]]` entry names a file and its digest, a project cannot add one, and a changed binary under its pin is refused rather than loaded

rules.title: An extension's classes are registered from its manifest at load, and a call into one is type-checked at compile time and emitted as a direct call
rules.diverges: a call into an extension is checked by `nvs check` like a call into `Core`, not dispatched by name at runtime

rules.title: A value crosses into an extension as the WIT type one closed table gives its Novis type, copied whole
A value crosses the guest boundary as a bounds-checked handle, never as a pointer
A guest is instantiated fresh for each request that calls it, so extension state cannot leak between requests
rules.diverges: a stateful PHP extension keeps its globals for the worker's lifetime; a guest starts pristine on every request and nothing it stored is there on the next one

rules.title: A guest call runs on its request's core as an async call the request's coroutine polls, and yields at every epoch tick
A guest runs under the request's CPU and memory caps, and a runaway guest traps rather than hanging a core
A guest's error result throws its mapped class, a trap throws `ExtensionError`, and only a CPU or memory limit is a `FATAL`
A guest has no ambient authority: WASI is not granted by default, and every host function it receives is capability-checked
rules.diverges: native extension code calls `open()` and `connect()` directly; a guest reaches the filesystem and the network only through the same grants script code has

rules.title: `nvs ext` creates, builds, inspects, tests, verifies and pins an extension, with Rust and C templates
An extension call costs a fixed ten-odd nanoseconds over a built-in call, so an extension's API is coarse-grained
A C dependency is admitted under ordinary audit only if attacker-controlled data never reaches it; otherwise it needs an exceptional verification record or is confined to wasm

sections.title: Running as a service
sections.blurb: An operator installs a service from the command line. The installer fails closed, and nothing about it is on the request path.

rules.title: PDF is a decode-only format of `nvs/image`, in the second wave, and never a member of `nvs/pdf`
rules.diverges: there is no Ghostscript to install and no ImageMagick policy to loosen; a page becomes an image through the same sandboxed component every other format uses

rules.title: `nvs service` is a namespace, and everything after a mandatory `--` is stored verbatim as the argv the service runs
rules.diverges: there is no shim — no NSSM, no WinSW, no hand-written unit around `php-fpm` — and the hosted program's own flags follow a `--` the installer never reads past

rules.title: The service installer fails closed: a closed `serve`/`run` allowlist, no relative path, no argv without `--config`, no password on a command line
rules.diverges: `sc create` and a hand-written unit store whatever they are given; the installer refuses each of these by name with an `E063x` diagnostic and installs nothing

rules.title: On Windows the argv is encoded into the SCM's one `ImagePath` string, the binary path is always quoted, and nothing else holds it
A service's default identity is the local system account, and `--account` names any other, the per-service virtual account included
rules.diverges: a hand-registered service runs as `LocalSystem`, and so does one installed here with no `--account`; the per-service virtual account and its grants are one `--account` away

rules.title: A stop drains, a `PARAMCHANGE` reloads, and the process's console and its lifecycle records go to the event log
rules.diverges: a shim can only report that the process exited; the service itself reports an advancing stop checkpoint and performs a reload in-process

rules.title: On Linux `nvs service unit` prints the systemd unit and touches nothing; writing it is an explicit `--install`
rules.diverges: the unit is generated rather than written by hand, and printing rather than installing is the default because configuration management owns the directory

rules.title: The generated unit carries the hardening block, `Type=notify`, `MemoryMax` from `[limits]`, and `AmbientCapabilities` only for a privileged port
rules.diverges: `NoNewPrivileges`, `ProtectSystem=strict` and an emptied `CapabilityBoundingSet` are emitted for you rather than left to whoever writes the unit

rules.title: A single-file bundle may not install itself as a service
There is no `Core\Service`: only an operator installs a service, from the command line, and nothing about it is on the request path

sections.title: Where Novis diverges
sections.blurb: Every departure from PHP is listed, and each exists because PHP left a binding untyped. Absent storage is never a zero value.

rules.title: Every departure from PHP's observable behaviour is listed as a divergence, and each exists only because PHP left a binding untyped
rules.diverges: the imported `.phpt` corpus passes at a structurally lower rate than a compatibility-first design would, and a failure in a listed class is intentional rather than a regression

rules.title: `->` on a receiver that can hold no object is refused where it is written
rules.diverges: `$i->name` on an `int` is a compile error (`E0495`) rather than a warning yielding `null`; only `mixed` keeps PHP's run-time answer, through a name-keyed fetch that throws

rules.title: Absent storage never reads as a zero value: an unassigned variable and `[]` in a read position are refused, and an absent key throws
rules.diverges: reading an undefined variable or an absent array key does not warn and yield `null`, and `$a[] .= "x"` does not append; `??`, `??=`, `isset` and `empty` keep PHP's answer

rules.title: An element write through a temporary is refused, because the separated copy has nowhere to be written back
rules.diverges: `f()[0] = 2` is `E0700` rather than a silently discarded write, and `(new Box())->rows[0] = 2` is accepted where PHP 8.5 refuses it

rules.title: A non-`void` body hands back a value at every exit; nothing returns `null` for a declaration it did not make
rules.diverges: a body that falls off its end is `E0739` and a written `return;` under a non-`void` declaration is `E0822`, each where it stands rather than a `null` return or a `TypeError` at run time

rules.title: A `return` never leaves a `finally` block, and neither does a `break` or `continue` whose target lies outside it
rules.diverges: `return` inside `finally` does not compile, instead of overriding the region's result and discarding a throw in flight (deprecated in 8.6)

rules.title: A constructor's `return` carries no value; a bare `return;` may still leave early
rules.diverges: `return $value;` in a constructor does not compile (deprecated in 8.6)

rules.title: A `readonly` property declares no default; a value known at the declaration is a `const`
rules.diverges: `readonly int $n = 1;` is refused where PHP 8.6 allows it

rules.title: Partial function application is not adopted; the closure literal already spells it
rules.diverges: PHP 8.6's `f(?, $x)` does not parse; write `fn($a) => f($a, $x)`

rules.title: `let` and `is` cannot name anything; `var` declares, `as` converts, and `is` is the type test
rules.diverges: `let` and `is` cannot name anything (deprecated as identifiers in 8.6), so a converted program renames them

rules.title: `instanceof` is refused where it is written, `is` is the one type test, and neither keyword is compared with PHP again
rules.diverges: PHP keeps `instanceof` beside the `is` it has reserved; Novis refuses the spelling outright and names the rewrite, and gives `$x is $cls` the dynamic class test PHP's Pattern Matching RFC leaves unclaimed

sections.title: Converting and completing PHP
sections.blurb: What the converter does with a trait or a shell call, and how every PHP built-in name stays a completion candidate.

rules.title: What PHP deprecates for removal is refused at compile time, never phased in behind a warning
rules.diverges: a PHP 8.6 deprecation is a compile error at the line it is written, with no deprecation channel and no warning

rules.title: `nvs convert` turns a stateless trait into an interface with defaults and a stateful one into a delegate, and names what it cannot decide
rules.diverges: `use T;` becomes `implements T`, a trait with state becomes a `{Trait}Impl` delegate flagged for review, and a trait `static` or a callback into the consuming class is a `TODO`

rules.title: `nvs convert` maps every PHP shell-execution call to `Core\Process` and flags each site, because a command string has no argv split
rules.diverges: `exec`, `system`, backticks, `shell_exec`, `passthru` and `proc_open` all become `Core\Process::run` or `spawn`, with a human supplying the executable path and the argv

rules.title: A session id the store did not issue is rejected, always, with no toggle
rules.diverges: `session.use_strict_mode` has no off position: an unknown, expired or attacker-minted id is discarded and a fresh one issued

rules.title: The PHP-name layer is joined once at build time, and a destination spelling the registry cannot place fails the build
Every PHP built-in name is a completion candidate, and the migration table is what the item says
rules.diverges: typing the PHP name you already know completes to the Novis member, and the PHP spelling never reaches a file

rules.title: A PHP-name completion item inserts only a `Core` member the registry already holds
rules.diverges: a suggestion whose destination is dropped, undecided or not built yet appears and inserts nothing, where a PHP editor completes any name it has indexed

rules.title: A PHP name completes only where a top-level identifier is legal, and sorts below every Novis symbol
rules.diverges: the PHP name is the fallback rather than the first suggestion, and it never appears after a receiver or a `::`

rules.title: `nvs.completion.phpNames` quiets or removes the PHP-name layer, and never touches `Core` completion
rules.diverges: the setting removes a reminder layer, never a spelling — no PHP name is ever an alias the program can reach
